exercises.prompt: Implement a class Counter that tracks an integer count. Its __init__ takes an optional start value that defaults to 0. It has three methods: inc() adds 1 to the count, dec() subtracts 1, and value() returns the current count. A new Counter() starts at 0, and after three inc() calls value() is 3. Separate Counter instances hold independent counts.

tests.setup:
a = Counter()
b = Counter()
a.inc()
a.inc()

hints: Store the count on the instance as self.count in __init__, then have each method read or change it through self.
inc() and dec() adjust self.count by 1 with += and -=, while value() returns it.
Set self.count = start in __init__ and use self.count += 1, self.count -= 1, and return self.count — because each new Counter() gets its own self.count, incrementing a stays invisible to b.

exercises.prompt: Implement a class Stack — a last-in, first-out collection. Its __init__ takes no arguments and starts empty. push(x) adds x on top; pop() removes and returns the top element; peek() returns the top element WITHOUT removing it; size() returns how many elements are stored. After push(1) then push(2), pop() returns 2. On a new empty stack size() is 0.
hints: Back the stack with a plain list on the instance — self.items = [] in __init__ — and let the list's own methods do the work.
list.append and list.pop already give last-in-first-out; peek reads the last element self.items[-1] without removing it, and size is len(self.items).
return self.items.pop() for pop and self.items[-1] for peek — peek must not call pop, or the size-after-peek test would drop to 1 instead of staying at 2.

exercises.prompt: Implement a class BankAccount. Its __init__ takes an optional starting balance that defaults to 0. deposit(amount) adds amount to the balance; withdraw(amount) subtracts amount but raises ValueError when amount is greater than the current balance (an overdraft); balance() returns the current balance. Withdrawing the exact balance is allowed and leaves 0. Separate accounts are independent.
hints: Keep the balance on the instance (self.bal), set from __init__'s start argument, and have each method read or adjust it.
In withdraw, guard first — if amount > self.bal: raise ValueError(...) — and only subtract when the funds are there; that raising line is what the raises tests exercise.

Use if amount > self.bal: raise ValueError('insufficient funds') before self.bal -= amount — the guard is > (not >=), so withdrawing exactly the balance succeeds and leaves 0, while over-withdrawing raises.

exercises.prompt: Using a dataclass, implement Rectangle with two fields, width and height. Add two methods: area() returns width × height, and perimeter() returns 2 × (width + height). For Rectangle(3, 4), area() is 12 and perimeter() is 14. Because it is a dataclass, two rectangles with the same fields compare equal: Rectangle(3, 4) == Rectangle(3, 4) is True. Decorate the class with @dataclass (from dataclasses import dataclass) so __init__ and equality are generated for you.
hints: @dataclass turns the two annotated fields, width: int and height: int, into a generated __init__ — so Rectangle(3, 4) just works — and you only write the two methods.
Inside the methods reach the fields through self: area() returns self.width * self.height, perimeter() returns 2 * (self.width + self.height).

With @dataclass, equality is generated to compare field-by-field, which is why Rectangle(3, 4) == Rectangle(3, 4) is True — a plain class (no dataclass) would compare by identity and that test would fail.

exercises.prompt: Implement a class Queue — a first-in, first-out collection. Its __init__ takes no arguments and starts empty. enqueue(x) adds x to the back; dequeue() removes and returns the front (oldest) element; size() returns how many elements are stored; is_empty() returns True when the queue has no elements and False otherwise. After enqueue(1) then enqueue(2), dequeue() returns 1 — the first one in.

tests.setup:
q = Queue()
q.enqueue(1)
q.enqueue(2)
q.dequeue()
q.dequeue()

hints: Back the queue with a list on the instance; the difference from a stack is which end you remove from.
enqueue adds to the back with append; dequeue removes from the FRONT with self.items.pop(0), giving first-in-first-out; is_empty checks whether len(self.items) is 0.
return self.items.pop(0) for dequeue — pop(0) removes the oldest element, so the first test returns 1; using self.items.pop() with no index would return 2 and turn the queue into a stack.
